tagline: River towns and migrating birds along Delaware’s two-lane Bayshore road
intro: South of New Castle, Route 9 runs through rural Delaware as a two-lane road west of the river and bay. DelDOT highlights coastal marshlands, wildlife, farming heritage and historic river towns along the Delaware Bayshore Byway, designated a National Scenic Byway in 2021. The older Route 9 Coastal Heritage corridor is now part of that longer journey, which continues south toward Lewes. The corridor lies within the Atlantic Flyway, where migrating shorebirds feed and rest each spring before continuing to northern breeding grounds.

The campaign began well before the new name: the state highway department recommended scenic status for Route 9 in 1965. Residents, public officials, nonprofit groups and agencies joined to nominate it in 2003; state designation followed in 2007. The byway took the Delaware Bayshore name in 2013, and DelDOT accepted its southern extension in 2017.

Driving south from New Castle, the road passes through the Delaware City refinery complex before reaching Delaware City and crossing the canal on Reedy Point Bridge. Beyond Port Penn, farms and wetlands lead toward the Odessa turnoff at Mathews Corners. Continue over Blackbird Creek and the Smyrna River, past the western side of Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge, then through Leipsic and Little Creek toward Dover Air Force Base.

moments.title: New Castle
moments.text: The courthouse cupola gives New Castle a place in the geometry of state borders: it is the center of the Twelve-Mile Circle defining much of Delaware’s boundary with Pennsylvania. The building was Delaware’s colonial capitol and first State House, and served as a courthouse until 1882. Government moved south to Dover in 1777; the county seat later moved to Wilmington. The Court House, Green and Sheriff’s House are now parts of First State National Historical Park. The town’s central green dates to the Dutch street plan. Route 9 itself bypasses the historic area on its passage through New Castle.
moments.notice: The courthouse cupola marks the center of the Twelve-Mile Circle.

moments.title: Odessa
moments.text: Before it became Odessa, the port was called Cantwell’s Bridge. In 1721, a son of Captain Edmund Cantwell opened a toll bridge across the creek here. The port shipped wheat, corn, tobacco and produce down Appoquinimink Creek to Delaware Bay and distant ports. When a railroad was proposed through town, merchants and vessel owners opposed it. The line went through Middletown instead, and the grain trade collapsed in 1855. Renaming the town Odessa, after the port in the Russian Empire, now Ukraine, was an effort to preserve its commercial future. A significant part of Odessa is now a historic district.

moments.title: Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Bombay Hook’s tidal marshes share the refuge with freshwater pools shaped by human work. Established in 1937 for migratory and wintering waterfowl, the refuge was purchased with federal duck stamp funds. Civilian Conservation Corps crews began work the following year, building a dike and a causeway to create three freshwater impoundments. Water levels in the pools are managed to encourage plants for waterfowl; drawing them down exposes mudflats where shorebirds and wading birds feed. The salt marsh, intersected by tidal streams and rivers, also serves as a nursery for marine organisms.
